claims.text: The starting composite contains distinct W particles or interconnected W ligaments dispersed in a Cu matrix.
Untreated W–Cu composites develop phase separation and interfacial voids under elevated-temperature and irradiation service conditions.
The proposed intervention is to coat W particles uniformly with an approximately 5 nm Ti layer before consolidation and sintering.
The Ti coating will induce a graded W–Ti–Cu interfacial region during consolidation.
The Ti-containing interfacial region will bond with both W and Cu.
The Ti-containing interfacial region will stabilize the interfacial microstructure.
The Ti-containing interfacial region will act as a diffusion barrier.
Reactive Ti will improve wettability between W and Cu.
The Ti transitional interphase will reduce W–Cu interfacial energy.
The Ti transitional interphase will limit fast diffusion paths.
Reduced interfacial energy and restricted diffusion will minimize void nucleation and phase separation under thermal and irradiation stress.
Suppression of interfacial voids and phase separation will yield higher thermal conductivity.
Under identical heat-transfer and irradiation conditions, Ti-coated W–Cu composites will have fewer interfacial voids than untreated composites.
Under identical heat-transfer and irradiation conditions, Ti-coated W–Cu composites will retain better phase integrity than untreated composites.
Under identical heat-transfer and irradiation conditions, Ti-coated W–Cu composites will have higher thermal conductivity than untreated composites.
The anticipated benefit is limited to processing routes that preserve the Ti coating, such as powder metallurgy with controlled sintering under an inert atmosphere.
The anticipated benefit applies at service temperatures up to approximately 500 °C and within the tested irradiation range.
